Abstract
This work introduces an exhaustive evaluation, including both benchmarks and real-
world data-intensive applications, performed in MareNostrum 4 and HPC4AI Labo-
ratory supercomputers using the Expand Ad-Hoc file system. Expand Ad-Hoc is an 
ad-hoc file system that dynamically virtualizes the local storage available on com-
pute nodes (i.e., SSD, SHM, etc.) into a fast storage volume to reduce congestion on 
parallel file systems used as backends in High-Performance Computing (HPC) envi-
ronments. The main contributions of this work include the design of a new ad-hoc 
parallel file system, called Expand Ad-Hoc, compatible with POSIX and MPI-IO, 
and an exhaustive and comprehensive evaluation of Expand. The evaluation com-
pares the performance obtained using IOR and DLIO benchmarks and Nek5000 and 
Remote Sensing real-world applications on Expand Ad-Hoc, GekkoFS, GPFS, and 
BeeGFS, showing satisfactory results proving that Expand Ad-Hoc can be used in 
HPC environments to improve the I/O performance of data-intensive applications 
transparently.

1  Introduction
In fields such as science, artificial intelligence, and big data, processing large 
amounts of data [1, 2] through workflows [3] is becoming increasingly common. 
Some examples of these applications include image analysis [4], forecasting weather 
[5], simulating turbulence [6], fluid dynamics [7], and modeling materials [8].
Because the traditional supercomputer architecture was initially designed for 
compute-intensive applications, supercomputers usually have more compute nodes 
than storage nodes. Moreover, the storage nodes are shared by all applications run-
ning on the supercomputer at the same time, and the associated data are accessed 
remotely from the compute node (see Fig. 1), with the I/O network shared by all 
applications accessing data [2]. This architecture can negatively impact the overall 
performance of data-intensive applications because frequent access to the applica-
tion data stored in the backend file system makes it a bottleneck.
Despite hardware improvements with SSD (solid-state drive) and PCM (phase 
change memory), as well as new approaches to storage architecture such as direct-
attached storage (DAS), network-attached storage (NAS), and storage area network 
(SAN), among other improvements, which can alleviate poor I/O performance, still, 
they are not enough [9].
To address these issues, ad-hoc file systems [10] have been proposed. Such file 
systems enable the creation of virtual partitions that utilize the local storage (disk or 
memory) of the compute nodes where applications are executed, serving as tempo-
rary file systems for one application. An ad-hoc file system provides data locality for 
the application, leading to decreased remote data access.
As a result of their tailored design, an ad-hoc file system offers several benefits:
•	 Data can be placed closer to the applications.
•	 Data stored in this file system do not need to be read from the backend file sys-
tem, reducing network use, interference with other applications, etc.

However, ad-hoc file systems have two main drawbacks that need to be addressed. 
On the one hand, every time an ad-hoc file system is used, it has to be deployed 
on the compute nodes; therefore, the application or workflow cannot start execution 
until the file system is deployed. On the other hand, if the application uses some ini-
tial data set or generates some output data, the ad-hoc file system must transfer these 
data between the backend file system and the ad-hoc file system, and vice versa.
Expand Ad-Hoc is an ad-hoc distributed and parallel file system that has been 
designed and optimized for data-intensive applications’ needs on supercomputers, 
leveraging data locality and simplified metadata management, among other features. 
Expand Ad-Hoc is linked to applications through a system call interception library, 
making the integration transparent to application programmers.
Expand Ad-Hoc offers the typical benefits of ad-hoc file systems. However, unlike 
other file systems, it allows changing the block size of the file system, implements 
optimizations to exploit data locality, and allows parallel I/O data staging. Expand 
Ad-Hoc uses MPI internally for client–server communication. MPI is a standard 
interface available on any supercomputing platform, and using MPI for communi-
cation opens the door to utilizing modern high-performance network technologies 
(libfabric, UCX, etc.) and switching between them to choose the one with the high-
est performance.
The primary distinction between Expand Ad-Hoc and other MPI-based I/O sys-
tems and libraries is that Expand Ad-Hoc provides a fully compatible and transparent 
POSIX and MPI-IO interface for all types of applications, not just MPI applications.
Additionally, this ad-hoc file system was developed as a file system for the 
ADMIRE [11] European project. The ADMIRE project seeks to develop a new soft-
ware stack capable of optimizing large-scale data I/O operations, reducing applica-
tion execution time, lowering costs, improving service quality, and enabling better 
energy efficiency when this software stack is used in conjunction.
This work introduces an exhaustive performance evaluation of Expand Ad-Hoc 
in MareNostrum 4 and HPC4AI Laboratory supercomputers, comparing the Gek-
koFS ad-hoc file system and the backend file systems available in these supercom-
puters (GPFS and BeeGFS, respectively) with Expand Ad-Hoc. In order to do that, 
both benchmarks and real-world applications have been used. In addition to properly 
understand the results of the performance evaluation performed, the main features of 
this ad-hoc file system will be described.
The main contributions of this paper are the following: 
1.	 The design of the Expand Ad-Hoc file system for High-Performance Computing 
(HPC) environments by focusing on the main features aimed at HPC environ-
ments. Expand Ad-Hoc offers a fully compatible and transparent POSIX and 
MPI-IO interface for all types of applications, not just MPI applications.
2.	 An exhaustive evaluation of the Expand Ad-Hoc file system in two different HPC 
environments using two benchmarks and two real-world applications, comparing 
the results obtained with those of three file systems.

2  Related work
Among the available storage solutions, parallel file systems are commonly used in 
the HPC area. Parallel file systems include ad-hoc file systems, which will also be 
discussed.
A parallel file system is a type of distributed file system that stores file informa-
tion between several servers, allowing parallel access to these files [12]. On those 
parallel file systems, from the full set of available nodes in the supercomputer, a sub-
set of those nodes is exclusively in charge of the shared data storage subsystem. This 
deployment causes I/O bottlenecks on these nodes because the file system shares 
these resources among all the jobs running on the supercomputer. Furthermore, it 
is a fixed subset of nodes, which limits its scalability in peak workloads [13]. Some 
well-known examples of parallel file systems are GPFS [14], Lustre [15], and 
BeeGFS [16].
Although the initial GPFS [14] parallel file system design from 1993 was planned 
for high-performance multimedia, it is also well suited for scientific computing. As 
a result, it is commonly used as a storage subsystem on supercomputers. One of its 
main features is a client-level data cache that allows I/O operations to be performed 
asynchronously, ensuring data coherence using a distributed lock manager. In addi-
tion, GPFS provides parallel access to files and allows adding or removing storage 
devices from the GPFS cluster while running without any further action.
Lustre [17] is a parallel file system that became the storage solution for large-
scale cluster computing after the introduction of Linux OS-based Beowulf clusters 
[18] as an alternative to expensive supercomputers. Lustre’s use was encouraged 
because it allows simultaneous read and write access to its files while using POSIX 
[19] semantics.
BeeGFS [16] is a parallel file system that started in 2005. It is specially designed 
for HPC use and is based on the POSIX interface. Furthermore, according to the 
authors, it is designed to maximize performance and scalability. To achieve this 
goal, BeeGFS splits the files into blocks and distributes them between all the storage 
nodes (like other parallel file systems do) and distributes the metadata to balance the 
load.
An ad-hoc file system allows the dynamic virtualization of the local storage on 
the compute nodes (HDD, SSD, etc.). That is, these file systems are deployed as 
soon as an application that uses this file system starts running. Therefore, the stor-
age resources available to the ad-hoc system will be the sum of the local resources 
of each compute node used by the application. This brings the storage closer to the

BurstFS [20] is an ad-hoc file system that was developed to be deployed as a local 
file system. It was one of the first of its kind. However, it has a significant draw-
back—the metadata are centralized in a metadata server, which causes bottlenecks.
Cruise [21] provides an in-memory file system with a subset of POSIX calls, 
especially for checkpointing in MPI applications. However, it does not provide a file 
system with a fully compliant POSIX interface.
The Distributed Asynchronous Object Storage (DAOS) [22] is an open-source, 
scalable file system designed to allow Storage Class Memory (SCM) and NVMe 
storage in user space. DAOS offers a key-value interface, as well as non-blocking 
transactional I/O, a versioned data model, and global snapshots. The DAOS storage 
API has native support for structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data mod-
els. In addition, it also offers direct support for MPI-IO and HDF5, as well as POSIX 
access for legacy applications for HPC applications. For data storage, DAOS stores 
metadata and small data in persistent memory and larger data on NVMe SSDs.
UnifyFS [23] is a file system designed for distributed storage access with a uni-
fied namespace. It is a user-level shared ephemeral file system that can adapt to 
different I/O workloads and storage devices. It also ensures that I/O interception 
is transparent. However, UnifyFS makes several trade-offs in its design, such as 
relaxing file permission checks and the consistency of the naming space hierarchy. 
This reduces the overhead of metadata management but affects the consistency of 
changes. Additionally, the log-based design means that it has the problems of this 
type of file system, such as growing memory, limited random I/O performance, and 
not being RAID-aware.
Another example of ad-hoc file systems is GekkoFS [27]. GekkoFS started in 
2017 and is currently under active development. As main features, this file system 
uses the RocksDB database [28] for metadata storage and the Mercury RPC interface 
[29] for communications. This file system uses a system call interception library, but 
the design used in the GekkoFS interception library does not ensure that all calls can 
be intercepted. For example, there are system calls, such as a file rename, that are 
not compatible with the GekkoFS design, which limits their use in existing appli-
cations. Furthermore, this file system has other problems related to using multiple 
dependencies of different software packages and specific versions of these. Depend-
ing on many different packages makes your design more fragile to changes in those 
packages, impacting performance (having to go through multiple software layers) 
and reliability (one change in any package can break the application).
BeeOND [25] is an ad-hoc file system that enables the user to dynamically deploy 
different instances of the BeeGFS file system [16]. Each instance inherits its ben-
efits, making it particularly useful in scenarios such as the cloud or using BeeGFS as 
a backend file system on supercomputers. BeeOND provides packages for a limited 
number of Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, and RHEL), which restricts its use.

3  Expand Ad‑Hoc file system
Expand1 is a parallel file system for heterogeneous clusters installed in user space, 
which facilitates its deployment in any POSIX-based environment [30, 31]. Expand 
works as a client–server architecture, building a distributed virtual partition across 
all the servers. When an application uses Expand as a file system, data are divided 
into blocks, whose size is defined at the virtual partition level, that are distributed in 
parallel among all the servers composing the distributed partition.
The first version of the Expand file system relied on standard servers and proto-
cols, such as Network File System (NFS), File Transfer Protocol (FTP), or GridFTP, 
which facilitated its integration in heterogeneous systems, as well as the reuse and 
aggregation of existing resources and parallel access to the data. Furthermore, it did 
not require server changes (e.g., NFS) because all data management was done on 
the client. To achieve this goal, Expand provided different connectors, allowing the 
creation of virtual partitions with diverse storage servers that implement different 
technologies, such as NFS, FTP, etc. For example, an NFS server and an FTP server 
could form a virtual partition, being transparent to the application that it was using 
Expand.
Over the years, Expand has evolved, and now this parallel and distributed file sys-
tem allows the use of its own servers that run in user space and exploit the local stor-
age of the compute nodes where they operate. Multiple communication protocols are 
supported in Expand nowadays: It has a specific server for distributed environments 
using sockets as a communication mechanism; for the Internet of Things (IoT) envi-
ronment, Expand provides a server based on the MQTT (Message Queuing Telem-
etry Transport) protocol; finally, for HPC, Expand provides MPI connectors.
This work will explain the design and implementation of the Expand Ad-Hoc file 
system for the HPC environment. To this aim, we have performed a complete rede-
sign of the initial Expand file system, using MPI for communications between cli-
ents and servers.

3.1  The design of Expand Ad‑Hoc file system
Expand Ad-Hoc file system architecture is based on a set of data servers running on 
different compute nodes that communicate with each other using MPI (see Fig. 3). 
We decided to use the MPI standard for communications because, since its appear-
ance in 1994, it has been heavily used in HPC. As a result, it is available in all super-
computers and is highly optimized for the different network technologies, following 
the MPI authors’ goals: performance, scalability, and portability. In addition, MPI 
has already been used in distributed storage systems [32], and current MPI imple-
mentations have been upgraded to support modern high-performance communica-
tion technologies such as libfabric, UCX, among others [33–35]. This allows MPI to 
remain a good choice for distributed storage systems.
As Expand Ad-Hoc is based on a client–server architecture, first, the Expand Ad-
Hoc servers must be run as an MPI application on the set of compute nodes allo-
cated to the application. If several application processes are run in one node, only 
one server is created in this node. Next, the application using the ad-hoc file system 
is deployed across all nodes with the Expand Ad-Hoc client. The way of deploying 
both elements using MPI communications is shown in Listing 1.

In Expand Ad-Hoc file system, local storage devices such as HDD, SSD, or 
shared memory on various servers deployed ad-hoc for an application are used 
to create distributed partitions. The goal is to store data near the application, thus 
reducing the need for remote access to the backend parallel file system. To store data 
locally, we rely on services provided by the local operating system, such as POSIX.
The application’s processes and the Expand Ad-Hoc servers might be deployed 
on the same compute nodes because Expand does not need dedicated storage serv-
ers. Although applications and servers run on the same compute nodes, their inter-
ference is minimal. This is because applications mainly perform computations, 
while ad-hoc servers mainly perform I/O. Furthermore, in operating systems, while 
a process is blocked waiting for an I/O operation, another process runs on the CPU. 
Hence, the I/O operations of ad-hoc servers and the computation of applications 
overlap. In addition, today’s multicore architectures help to alleviate this problem 
for two reasons: There is a large number of cores available for both the ad-hoc serv-
ers and the application, and it is possible to pin more cores to the application, if 
required, with minimal interference to the ad-hoc server.
This is the recommended deployment because it minimizes the number of 
accesses to remote data. Nevertheless, the processes of the application and the 
Expand Ad-Hoc servers can be deployed on different compute nodes if needed. Fig-
ure 3 shows both alternatives.

3.3  Data distribution
Expand Ad-Hoc file system combines multiple servers to create a distributed virtual 
partition, where each server provides one or more directories merged to create the 
partition on a particular compute node. The files in a virtual partition are split into 
blocks, which will then be distributed among all the Expand Ad-Hoc servers that are 
associated with that partition. Thus, each server will hold a portion of the original 
file, which is called a subfile. A file stored in Expand Ad-Hoc is the set of subfiles on 
the servers. Those subfiles are transparent to the users.
To distribute the blocks equally among all the deployed ad-hoc servers, a cyclic or 
“round-robin” pattern is followed. This distribution pattern has been chosen because 
it allows an equitable distribution of the workload among all servers, as well as ena-
bling parallel I/O. Figure 5 shows the way the blocks are distributed among the sub-
files in the distributed virtual partition.
3.4  Metadata and directory management
Expand Ad-Hoc does not use any kind of metadata manager to simplify the file nam-
ing process and reduce potential bottlenecks in the metadata server. The Expand Ad-
Hoc clients are responsible for metadata management, which is split into two levels: 
metadata associated with the file and metadata associated with Expand Ad-Hoc sub-
file management.
In the metadata associated with the file, we find the corresponding POSIX meta-
data, such as size, date, permissions, owner, etc. Those metadata are managed by the 
local file system of each node and are therefore distributed among all nodes. In this 
way, the metadata management is distributed among all nodes, avoiding bottlenecks 
in a single node. On the one hand, to retrieve most of the attributes of a file, it is only 
necessary to consult the metadata from one subfile. However, some file attributes,

When a subfile is accessed, the Expand Ad-Hoc library uses the virtual file han-

that are sent to the servers involved. This way, if k ad-hoc servers are involved in a 
request, Expand Ad-Hoc can perform k requests simultaneously to the servers using

3.6  I/O data staging
If an application needs initial data when using an ad-hoc file system, data staging 
is needed to preload (stage-in) data from the backend file system (e.g., GPFS) to 
the ad-hoc file system servers. The transfer of data between the backend file system 
and Expand Ad-Hoc file system is done through an MPI program that runs on the 
Expand Ad-Hoc servers. This program creates a replicated directory tree and the 
subfile in parallel on each server for every file stored in the backend.
Likewise, when the application that uses the ad-hoc file system finalizes its exe-
cution, persistent data must be stored in the backend file system because the ad-hoc 
servers will no longer be available. To complete this task, a flush operation (stage-
out) is provided to move data from the Expand Ad-Hoc servers to the backend file 
system. In Expand Ad-Hoc, an MPI program, similar to the one mentioned earlier, 
is used for this data transfer. The program runs on the ad-hoc servers and reads in 
parallel subfiles stored in the servers, generating the file that will be saved in the 
backend file system.
Furthermore, the flush operation can also be used during the application execu-
tion to store the generated data persistently in the backend file system. Therefore, 
this operation helps mitigate data loss if a software or hardware issue occurs during 
the application execution. Moreover, as this operation is performed on demand, if 
the data generated by the application are temporary, then by skipping this operation, 
we avoid the potential overhead caused by its execution.
Figure 4 shows both preload and flush operations.
3.7  Data locality
As explained in Sect. 3.1, Expand Ad-Hoc servers can be executed on the compute 
nodes where the parallel application is being run. When this occurs, the application 
data are distributed among all compute nodes. In some cases, this allows access to 
the data requested by an application process using the local file system of the com-
pute node by executing this process in the same node where the data are stored (see 
arrow tagged as “Local Access” in Fig. 4). This helps to optimize data access from 
the Expand Ad-Hoc client and avoids delays and network-related issues that might 
occur when using remote data access.
It is important to keep in mind that data locality is crucial when multiple parallel 
applications (workflows) need to process the same dataset on the same nodes.

3.8  System call interception
Expand Ad-Hoc offers a fully compliant POSIX and MPI-IO interface. With this 
aim, Expand Ad-Hoc provides a POSIX system call interception library that allows 
the use of Expand Ad-Hoc without modifying the source code of existing or legacy 
applications. This library intercepts the POSIX system calls made while a program 
is running. If a file is stored in Expand Ad-Hoc, which is detected because the file 
pathnames include the Expand Ad-Hoc mount point, the corresponding Expand Ad-
Hoc API function is called. However, if the system call is made on the compute 
node’s local file system, the corresponding libc.so system call will be executed 
(see Fig. 4).
To load the intercept library before everything else, including the Linux libc.
so, without needing super-user permissions, we have chosen to use LD_PRELOAD. 
Although there are other technologies to perform the same operation, such as FUSE 
[39], FUSE uses a block size of 128 KiB, which limits the block size of the ad-hoc 
file system to this value. Furthermore, FUSE is in the Linux kernel and requires 
super-user permissions, making it difficult to use, especially in HPC environments.
Also, Expand Ad-Hoc provides a native API with functions that are very similar 
to the POSIX API calls, both in their names (e.g., xpn_open, xpn_read, etc.) 
and in the arguments they receive (e.g., xpn_read(fd, buf, nb)). To use the 
Expand Ad-Hoc API, the source code must be altered, and the application must be 
compiled with the Expand Ad-Hoc dynamic library.

As a summary of the evaluation carried out with the benchmark IOR, on the one 
hand, Expand Ad-Hoc globally performs better than the GekkoFS ad-hoc file system

the other hand, Expand Ad-Hoc also performs better than parallel file systems GPFS

compute nodes, taking advantage of data locality and the operating system cache, 
allowing the opportunity to scale with the number of compute nodes.

it exploits the possible optimizations that it provides, for example, the use of cach-
ing. Furthermore, regardless of the storage device used, the local file system is 
always used, so it may introduce an overhead and, therefore, not take advantage of 
the full hardware bandwidth. As a result, read operations when using SSD and SHM 
devices in Expand Ad-Hoc achieve very similar results in read operations.
Due to the Expand Ad-Hoc design, each compute node can become a storage 
server. Therefore, if an application requires a large number of compute nodes to run, 
Expand Ad-Hoc can be adapted for this workload. Unlike GPFS and BeeGFS, which 
have a fixed storage server configuration, which can lead to bottlenecks, as discussed 
in Sect. 1. Expand Ad-Hoc takes advantage of the modular and efficient design of 
MPI communications, which allows working with the best high-performance mod-
ule available on each platform (UCX, libfabric, etc.).

5  Conclusions and future work
This work presented the Expand Ad-Hoc parallel file system and its feasibility for 
improving the I/O performance of HPC environments. For this purpose, the Expand 
Ad-Hoc design has been described, and an exhaustive evaluation has been conducted 
on MareNostrum 4 and HPC4AI Laboratory supercomputers using IOR and DLIO 
benchmarks, as well as the Nek5000 and Remote Sensing real-world applications.
The Expand Ad-Hoc file system uses ad-hoc data servers running on the same 
compute nodes where the application is executing. Moreover, Expand Ad-Hoc file 
system uses the local storage available on the compute node. This local storage 
could be HDD/SSD, or in systems that do not have local storage in the compute 
nodes, but do have shared memory, shared memory can be employed (SHM through 
/dev/shm).
This study shows that using MPI-based data servers and locality in the design of 
Expand Ad-Hoc file system can improve scalability and increase throughput when 
performing I/O operations simultaneously on one or more files.
In real-world applications, we have also seen how Expand Ad-Hoc can substan-
tially reduce the execution time, taking into account even the time for stage-in. For 
example, in the Nek5000 fluid dynamics application, the time step data write inter-
val can be reduced without impacting the total execution time. This allows the post-
processing of simulation data to be much more accurate.
The main contributions of this work are:
•	 An ad-hoc file system design especially targeted for running data-intensive appli-
cations in HPC environments.

The main contributions of the Expand Ad-Hoc design are:
•	 The ad-hoc architecture allows customizing the file system to the application, 
contrary to backend file systems in which a fixed number of I/O nodes are used.
•	 Expand Ad-Hoc can be used exclusively by one application, contrary to backend 
file systems shared by all applications, leading to interference.
•	 Expand Ad-Hoc takes advantage of data locality, preventing remote access when 
the data is on the same compute node as the application. This is especially ben-
eficial when running workflows on this file system because different workflow 
tasks use to access the same data set.
•	 Expand Ad-Hoc is based on a client–server architecture, using MPI servers 
for HPC environments. Current MPI implementations have been improved to 
include modern high-performance communication technologies such as libfabric 
and UCX, among others. It is possible to choose for Expand Ad-Hoc the MPI 
communication module that best fits, while in other distributed storage solutions, 
this choice is fixed and unique.
For all these reasons, the Expand Ad-Hoc design is particularly convenient for data-
intensive applications in the HPC environments because it prevents overhead in 
backend file systems such as GPFS or BeeGFS.
Our future work includes designing support for malleability and evaluating its 
performance. We also aim to provide fault tolerance through block replication for 
the Expand Ad-Hoc file system, but without recovery mechanisms at this time. We 
intend to include a data replacement algorithm in Expand Ad-Hoc, because we 
assume in the current version that there will be enough free space for the application 
data. We plan to test Expand Ad-Hoc file system with other real-world applications.

Abstract: This work introduces an exhaustive evaluation, including both benchmarks and real- world data-intensive applications, performed in MareNostrum 4 and HPC4AI Labo- ratory supercomputers using the Expand Ad-Hoc file system. Expand Ad-Hoc is an ad-hoc file system that dynamically virtualizes the local storage available on com- pute nodes (i.e., SSD, SHM, etc.) into a fast storage volume to reduce congestion on parallel file systems used as backends in High-Performance Computing (HPC) envi- ronments. The main contributions of this work include the design of a new ad-hoc parallel file system, called Expand Ad-Hoc, compatible with POSIX and MPI-IO, and an exhaustive and comprehensive evaluation of Expand. The evaluation com- pares the performance obtained using IOR and DLIO benchmarks and Nek5000 and Remote Sensing real-world applications on Expand Ad-Hoc, GekkoFS, GPFS, and BeeGFS, showing satisfactory results proving that Expand Ad-Hoc can be used in HPC environments to improve the I/O performance of data-intensive applications transparently.
